items.topic: Wheeling trades as a volatility play
items.definition: A wheeling trade rents transmission capacity to physically move power from a low-volatility market to a high-volatility market, capturing the price swings that occur when the two regions' marginal fuels have very different volatility profiles.
items.core_idea: Renting a transmission line behaves like buying an option: the renter pays an upfront cost for the right to move power, and profits when price divergence between the two markets is large enough to justify shipping power from the cheap/stable region to the volatile one.
key_points: Works best when the two connected regions have different marginal fuels with different price volatility (e.g., coal-marginal Midwest vs. gas-marginal South).
Even if average power prices are similar in both regions, the more volatile region will periodically spike, creating windows where exporting power from the calmer region is profitable.

Profit is realized by making many spot-market trades to exploit these periodic windows, plus seasonal futures trades where predictable weather-driven demand differences exist (e.g., earlier/longer hot season in the South).
The line owner/renter can hedge the position by selling natural gas options or locking in seasonal futures, since the position is structurally long volatility.
Execution requires a long-term rental contract plus, for every physical transfer, scheduling of delivery, transmission, and sale — creating significant operational overhead.
relationships: Analogous to holding a long option on the volatile region's marginal fuel price
trading_implications: The main risk is overpaying for the transmission rental — the same risk profile as overpaying an option premium.
Substantial operational risk exists because every trade requires physically scheduling deliveries and transmission, not just a financial position.
A trading desk needs the capability to handle scheduling and paperwork for physical transactions, not just financial execution.
common_misunderstandings: The trade is not primarily a bet on average price levels being different between regions — it is a bet on relative volatility, since it can be profitable even when average prices are similar.

items.topic: Location spread trades as the financial analog of wheeling
items.definition: A location spread trade is a purely financial position — long futures/forwards in one pricing hub and short in another — that speculates on the relative price relationship between two regions without any physical transmission or delivery of power.
items.core_idea: When physical transmission between two markets doesn't exist (so power bought in one market can't be resold in another), traders can still take a view on the two markets' relative prices by trading offsetting long/short futures positions and settling in cash.
key_points: Without available transmission, all power purchased in a market must be resold into that same market — physical arbitrage between the two regions is impossible.
A location spread substitutes a financial bet for the missing physical link: long one region's futures, short the other's.
Positions are typically closed out (liquidated) before physical delivery is required, since there is no transmission to actually move power to settle the obligation in the other region.
These trades profit when the actual price relationship between the two regions at settlement differs from what the market expected when the trade was initiated.
Location spreads are operationally simpler than wheeling trades: no physical purchase/sale, no scheduling, everything settles in cash.
The tradeoff is that a location spread cannot deliver power from one region to meet an obligation in another — the physical-delivery benefit of wheeling is lost.
Traders compare physical (wheeling) and financial (spread) alternatives to find the lowest-cost way to express a similar market view.
relationships: Financial substitute for a wheeling trade when no transmission is available
trading_implications: Lower operational risk than wheeling since there's no physical scheduling, but also no ability to physically deliver power to cover another region's obligation.
Must be unwound via offsetting trades before futures expiration/physical delivery, unlike a wheeling trade which can actually deliver power.
common_misunderstandings: A location spread is not equivalent in payoff structure to a wheeling trade — it lacks the option-like optionality that comes from actually owning the right to physically move power.

items.definition: A price spread is simply the price in one region minus the price in another region, collapsing two separate regional prices into a single comparative number.
items.core_idea: Spreads express relative value between two markets as one number, which is what a location spread trade is designed to speculate on.
key_points: Example given: if New York price is $100 and California price is $120, the New York/California spread is -$20.
The sign and magnitude of the spread convention (Region A minus Region B) matters for interpreting which side of the trade is long or short.

variables.Price(A): spot or futures price in region A
variables.Price(B): spot or futures price in region B

trading_implications: A location spread position is a bet that this difference will move in a particular direction relative to market expectations at trade inception.

items.topic: Wheeling trade example: Midwest coal to Gulf Coast gas
items.definition: A worked example of renting transmission between the coal-marginal Midwest and the gas-marginal southern U.S. to exploit the South's higher price volatility.
items.core_idea: Because Wyoming coal keeps Midwest power prices stable while southern U.S. power prices track volatile natural gas, a transmission line between the two lets a trader export power from the Midwest whenever southern prices spike.
key_points: Low-cost, abundant Wyoming coal makes coal the marginal (price-setting) fuel in the Midwest, keeping power prices there relatively stable.
Most southern U.S. plants burn natural gas, whose price is much more volatile than coal, so southern power prices swing more.

Seasonal timing matters: hot weather starts earlier and lasts longer in the South, creating predictable seasonal windows (importing from a cool Midwest into a hot South) that can be captured with futures rather than only spot trades.
Execution requires a direct long-term rental contract between the two parties plus per-transaction scheduling of delivery, transmission, and sale.
High operational risk is inherent because of the physical scheduling burden on every transfer.
trading_implications: The position can be hedged by selling natural gas options or locking in seasonal futures since the exposure is structurally long gas-price volatility.
Biggest risk is overpaying for the transmission rental itself, analogous to overpaying an option premium.

items.topic: Location spread trade example: NP-15 vs. MID-C on an early snowmelt view
items.definition: A worked example of a March location spread between California (NP-15) and the Pacific Northwest (MID-C) built on a forecast of an earlier-than-normal Cascade snowmelt.
items.core_idea: A trader who believes government meteorologists' early-thaw forecast is correct, and that the market hasn't priced it in, goes long NP-15 and short MID-C futures to bet that California prices will be relatively higher than Pacific Northwest prices for March.
key_points: Normally, Pacific Northwest power prices hit their seasonal low in April when Cascade snowmelt forces hydro dams to run at full capacity around the clock to avoid flooding, regardless of demand — this generation cannot be curtailed.
The trader's thesis: forecast warm Pacific water temperatures will bring an early thaw, pulling this low-price, must-run hydro period earlier than the market expects.
Trade structure: buy NP-15 peak power futures (long California) and sell MID-C peak power futures (short Pacific Northwest) for the March contract.

A key risk the author flags: natural gas is the marginal fuel in California, so if gas prices fall, California power prices fall too, working against the long NP-15 leg independent of the snowmelt thesis.

The author also questions the spread structure itself: an early warm front and cheap Columbia River hydro power is more likely to push California prices down than up, suggesting an outright short MID-C position might carry less risk than the spread.
Because there is no transmission link being used, the position must be closed by an offsetting futures trade before expiration — it cannot be settled by physically delivering power.
relationships: Depends on marginal-fuel price transmission (gas -> California power)
trading_implications: Profit or loss is realized only if futures prices move in the expected direction by the time the position is liquidated, and liquidation must occur before contract expiration.
A directional (outright) trade can sometimes be a lower-risk expression of a market view than a spread, if the two legs' expected price responses to the same event are not actually offsetting.
common_misunderstandings: Choosing a spread trade isn't automatically lower risk than an outright position — if the underlying event is expected to move both legs in the same direction, the spread structure itself may be the wrong trade design.
related_topics: Location spread trades as the financial analog of wheeling
